newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. urged to freeze Bosnia war criminals' assets.
newsitem.headline: U.N. urged to freeze Bosnia war criminals' assets.

text.p: The international community's representative in Bosnia proposed Monday tracing and freezing the assets of war criminals and other corrupt figures impeding implementation of the 1995 Dayton peace accords.

After briefing the Security Council, former Spanish Foreign Minister Carlos Westendorp told reporters he had suggested the establishment of "an inter-agency unit to fight against corruption" in Bosnia, comprising international and local officials.

"I have also said to the Security Council that it would be very useful to study the possibility of tracing out the assets of war criminals and other crooks who are acting in the country in order to identify them and freeze them through an international action."

Westendorp said the havens for such assets were well known and the council should "reflect on that possibility and at a certain moment bring a resolution in order to be able to trace these assets all over the world."

He did not name any alleged war criminals but two of the most prominent persons indicted by the Hague-based U.N. war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his military commander, General Ratko Mladic. Both are still at large.

Westendorp was Spain's U.N. ambassador before being appointed May 30 as the international community's High Representative for Bosnia, responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Balkan peace process.

Asked what kind of cooperation would be needed from governments to trace the assets of war criminals and others, he said: "A similar cooperation as the banks and authorities in different countries are having for the so-called Jewish gold in the Second World War. To trace it out and to identify to whom those assets belong and then to freeze them."
Not only Switzerland was involved, he said, adding: "It is all over the world. We don't know exactly, but people speak about the Channel Islands, Cyprus, north and south Lebanon, whatever."
Regarding delays in carrying out the Dayton accords, he said that in the Republika Srpska, the Bosnian Serb entity, "the same leaders who made war are still leading the country."
The only way to change the leaders was through free and fair elections, and this required free media and the restructuring of the police so they did not intimidate the population.

He noted that an Aug. 1 deadline was approaching for the completion of a number of actions, including confirmation of Bosnia's ambassadors by the country's presidency and enactment of laws on citizenship and passports.
"Bosnia-Herzegovina is never going to be normal while the war criminals are at large, so the parties have to comply with Dayton and send the indicted persons to The Hague," he said.
The media in the Bosnian Moslem-Croat Federation were "somewhat freer," he said, adding: "There are more opposition parties and the editorial approach is freer than in Republika Srpska."
